title: Can the President Fire the Heads of Independent Agencies?
hook: For 91 years, a 1935 precedent shielded independent agency heads from being fired at a president's will. In 2026 the Supreme Court swept most of that shield away.
key_points: Independent agencies like the FTC were long run by officials Congress shielded from at-will presidential removal.
That shield traced to Humphrey's Executor (1935), a 91-year-old Supreme Court precedent.
In 2026's Trump v. Slaughter, a 6-3 Court overturned it, letting the president fire an FTC commissioner.
The ruling endorses 'unitary executive theory': that all executive power belongs to the president alone.
The Court carved out the Federal Reserve, leaving its removal protections intact for now.
content_html: For nine decades, a single Supreme Court precedent has stood between a U.S. president and the heads of agencies meant to operate at arm's length from the White House. In June 2026, much of that precedent fell.
extra_html: The 1935 case Humphrey's Executor v. United States held that Congress could shield certain independent-agency officials — commissioners at bodies like the Federal Trade Commission — from being fired by the president except for cause, such as neglect or malfeasance. As NPR's Andrea Hsu reports, a 6-3 Supreme Court in Trump v. Slaughter overturned that precedent, allowing the president to remove an FTC commissioner at will. SCOTUSblog described the decision as overturning "a major restraint on presidential power." Commentary in The Conversation frames the ruling as effectively endorsing the unitary executive theory — the view that all executive power the Constitution grants belongs to the president alone, leaving little room for Congress to insulate any executive officer from presidential control. Notably, the Court left one major exception standing: SCOTUSblog also reported that a Federal Reserve governor's removal protections survived, on the theory that the Fed's unique structure sets it apart from ordinary regulatory agencies. The case is a clean illustration of how a single doctrinal shift in the removal power can rebalance the separation of powers itself — expanding the executive branch's control at the expense of checks Congress once built into the bureaucracy.

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: The Executive
related.hook: Laws don't enforce themselves. The executive is the branch that runs the state day to day — carrying out the law, commanding the bureaucracy, and acting in a crisis.

related.title: Checks and Balances
related.hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

flashcards.prompt: What did Humphrey's Executor (1935) protect, and what happened to it in 2026?
flashcards.back_html: It let Congress shield independent-agency heads, like FTC commissioners, from being fired at will. In 2026's Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court overturned that precedent.

flashcards.prompt: What theory does the Trump v. Slaughter ruling effectively endorse?

choices.text: Unitary executive theory — that all executive power belongs to the president alone
Judicial supremacy — that courts control how agencies are run
Nullification — that states can override federal agency rules

flashcards.explanation_html: The ruling gives the president broad removal power over executive officers, consistent with the view that the Constitution vests all executive power in the president alone.

flashcards.prompt: Which agency did the Court leave outside the scope of its 2026 removal-power ruling?
flashcards.explanation_html: The Court let a Federal Reserve governor's removal protections stand, treating the Fed's structure as distinct from agencies like the FTC.
